lede: How these games are actually decided. Patience plus PLW rules — not baseball habits. Keep it in the book so we play the same way.
why: Walks knock pitchers out of the game. Heat in the zone is a ball. Defense is a 5-second throw in the air. That is what Adam Tanic and Tom Gannon keep winning with.
source: From 150 PLW broadcasts (~431 hours) on YouTube, 2020–2026, plus recap shows. Live games are on twitch.tv/premierwiffle. Auto-captions are messy; quotes are cleaned from the booth.
rules: Called strikes must read ≤55 mph and hit the K-zone in the air.
Walk 2 batters → pitcher is done (last eligible pitcher has no walk cap).
No gloves. Force outs: ball into backstop / K-zone / batter in the air within 5 seconds.
Only official yellow Wiffle bats. Legal tape only.
Motto: Play Hard. Have Fun. Respect All.

voices.name: Adam Tanic
voices.blurb: Patient to a fault: takes the first-pitch walk, red-light on 3–1, waits for ~49 mph, then goes opposite field. That oppo/middle look is how he avoids getting jammed — pitchers know it and still work him inside, so he makes midgame adjustments. As manager he stacks a table-setter in front of himself for RBIs. On the mound he throws strikes and lives on defense. Once the league got star-heavy, cookies with nobody on stopped working — locate and get ahead.

voices.name: Tom Gannon
voices.blurb: The eye the announcers point at when they teach the two-walk rule. Takes the close 3–2 rather than expand. Changes speeds, hides the full arsenal early so the league does not get a scouting report, and works the bottom of the K-zone. One walk can settle you. Two still ends the night.

playbook.title: Hitting
items: Start every AB as if it is 0–2 mentally — it is already 0–1.
Do not swing at 55+ even if it looks like a strike. Sit ~49.
3–0 / 3–1 with nobody out: red light. Make him throw a strike.
Protect with two strikes, but a chase-and-whiff on 3–2 is how rallies die.
Walks move the lineup and knock starters out. Solos alone rarely win.
Opposite field is live. Tanic’s homers in these tapes are often the other way.
Not getting jammed is the other half of hitting. Hands inside, sit back, let it travel. See Don't get jammed below.

playbook.title: Pitching and defense
items: Live under 55 with movement. Screwballs and sliders dominate the booth talk.
Speed vs home runs: do not live at 55 or 37. Mix, and never groove the speed they are sitting on. See Speed vs home runs below.
Jam hitters: finish on the hands so they cannot extend. See Jam batters below.
Work the bottom of the 24×28.5 K-zone. Low misses are balls you survive.
Walk one: get timid, throw strikes. Walk two: you are done.
Do not show every pitch in game 1 of a season or a series.
Fielding is a 5-second throw, not baseball. Knock it down, in the air, to the wall. See Fielding below.
An ace who cannot give you nine innings on a night leaves game 3 exposed.

playbook.title: Jam batters
items: Jam means throw inside so they cannot get the barrel out. Success is off the fist, no extension, a popup or a weak punch in the air.
Live on the inside half. Slider, screw, or two-seam that tunnels then buries on the hands last second — still under 55.
Finish on the fists, never the heart of the plate. Miss middle-in and that is the pitch they extend on.
After they just pulled one, jam the next swing. They are already thinking pull.
Lefty vs lefty: jam so they cannot open up. Leave it out over the plate and it goes over the container.
Change eye levels after you show inside — in, then down.
A jammed yellow bat can still flare. Off the hands is not always an out. Crowd the plate and miss the hands, it can be two runs.
If they sit oppo and keep their hands inside, a jam that does not actually finish on the fists is their barrel. Finish in, or mix away so they cannot sit inside.

playbook.title: Don't get jammed
items: Tanic's MO is sit back, let it travel, and look middle / opposite field. Pitchers work him inside because they know that. He still does it, then adjusts mid-game when they overcommit in.
Keep your hands inside the ball and close to your body. Do not swing the yellow bat like a baseball bat — drag it, don't turn and pull.
Stay back. The light bat gets you out in front of everything. Let it come so you can recognize the screw that starts middle then darts to your hands.
Do not dive in and reach for a pitch that looks away. That is how you get trapped: it comes back in, you are jammed, you roll over to short or pop it up.
Stay inside 12-to-6 and up-and-in too. If you don't, it rips foul. If you do, you can still poke it.
For pitchers: a hitter who sits oppo with quiet hands will barrel your 'jam' unless it actually gets to the fists. That's why location on the hands matters more than throwing inside-ish.

playbook.title: Speed vs home runs
items: Neither 55 nor 37 is safe by itself. A home run is a hitter on time in the heart of the plate. Groove either speed down the middle and it is a cookie.
55 down the pipe is the classic home-run pitch. Near the cap the ball has less time to move, so a straight 55 is batting practice. Hitters are sitting ~49.
37 / a floating 40 is only hard if they cheat and get out in front. Good hitters sit back. A hanging slow one middle is a donut — they wait and go oppo, over the container.
Use the gap, not one number. Live ~48–53 with actual break. Show 55 as the fast look, then take 4–8 mph off with the same arm. A 51 vs 55 got Tanic out in front instead of oppo.
Change of speed can fool them even when location does not. Changeups exist to get a loud swing out in front.
Never lay a cookie 3–2 with traffic. Walk and go to the next arm rather than a three-run hanger.
After they just missed one out front, do not come back middle at the speed they sat on. Jam, bury it, or change eye level.

playbook.title: Fielding
items: Nobody runs to first. The clock is the runner. Starts when the ball is in the hitting area. Stops at the backstop / K-zone / a force bag. 4.99 is an out. 5.00 is safe.
You do not have to field it clean. Knock it down and throw immediately, in the air. A short hop in front of the wall is an error.
The backstop is first. On a normal grounder you have the whole wall, or the K-zone, or the batter if you hit him in the air. Do not run to first. Stay out of the throwing lane.

Double play: tag second (or third if that is the force), then if you still have time hit the middle panel of the backstop — between the two pipes — or the K-zone. Regular first-base throws can use the whole wall; the DP throw cannot.
First and second / bases loaded: cheapest two outs are step on third, throw to second. First only if time. No third baseman means you cannot go that way — take the sure out.
Miss low, not over the top. Over the backstop is extra bases. Through the infield or an outfielder touching it is already a single — live with it.

Fly ball with nobody on third: catch it. Bare hands. High ones are harder than baseball. Tag from third is the only time anyone actually runs — cutoff is legal; get the ball to the backstop or K-zone in the air before he touches home. Do not airmail it over the wall.

quotes.quote: Working that slider inside to righties and jamming them up and not letting them get any extension on the ball and they're just kind of punching it up in the air.
We jammed him. The difference was keeping the ball in on his hands now versus game one was over the plate a little more. He's looking to get extended.
Ooh, jams him on that screw ball. Kind of got buried on his hands last second. He just hit a home run to the right side, so he's up there already thinking pull again — then that ball jammed him.
Lefty versus lefty — definitely gonna try to jam him a little bit. If you leave it to him opening up, there's gonna be a wiffle ball over the container.
See if Macabee can jam him here. Oh he jammed it right back — definitely pitched inside on that one. Changing the eye levels.
quotes.who: Gannon in the booth · Warbirds @ Snappers

quotes.tip: Tanic sits oppo — so they jam him
quotes.quote: Look for Tanic going opposite field right here. He always makes midgame adjustments. I think for the most part they've worked him inside. They know Tanic's MO of looking to go up the middle or left. They kind of want to jam him a little bit.

Screwball right in the middle of the plate, then an eight-inch sharp turn inside. He's diving in trying to go the other way and all of a sudden it's on your hands and you get jammed. You think it's out over the plate, you reach for it, and it traps you. Good hitters keep their hands close to the body and get some bat on it.
Good job keeping his hands inside the ball there — not getting out, not turning like a baseball bat, just kind of dragging.

quotes.tip: Sit back and let it travel
quotes.quote: The hardest thing is being able to sit back. That little light bat — you can be out in front of a ton. Sitting back and letting it come opened me up a little bit, allowed me to see it, let it travel.
Keeps his hands inside the ball. Stay inside the ball and poke it. First and second, it's a home run or strikeout situation — or oppo.

quotes.tip: 55 down the pipe is a home-run pitch
quotes.quote: That was a home run pitch — 55 down the pipe. That could have went dead center for that solo shot.
quotes.who: Bombers series · Kyle Lohman on the mound

quotes.tip: Four mph gets them out front
quotes.quote: Little change up. 51 is a huge difference in 55 — just a little out front.
It's all about deception in this league when you have a 55 mile an hour max. Deception and change of speed is so key.
quotes.who: Booth · change of speed with a 55 cap

quotes.quote: You just can't throw cookies in this league anymore. You can't just lay a cookie up there 3–2. Walking him and loading the bases is just fine — cannot give the cookie three-run home run. Sharp strikes, not these hangers.

quotes.tip: Slow is a bomb if they wait
quotes.quote: So slow that they're so far out in front. Low 40s. They see you only got the one pitch so they're just waiting for it to break. It's hard to hit those slow balls — if he throws him another strike it's going to be hit over the container.
quotes.who: James Perez at the plate · low 40s

quotes.quote: Swung so early on that. The location didn't matter — he was just completely fooled by the speed. If you can start thinking out there on the mound you can kind of get the hitter out in front of you.

quotes.tip: Two walks and you are done
quotes.quote: What an eye — takes that walk, that's huge. Two walks in the PLW you cannot pitch the rest of the game. Close pitch, but a discerning eye from the veteran Tom Gannon.
He's got to get that down. Low strike zone too — so you can get away with a lot of pitches that are very low.
quotes.who: Gannon in the booth · Warbirds @ Snappers

quotes.tip: Take the walk if you have to
quotes.quote: Greg is going to have to get one over the plate if he wants to stay in this game. You take the walk if you have to.
quotes.who: Gannon in the booth · Warbirds @ Snappers

quotes.tip: Over 55 is a ball even in the zone
quotes.quote: A little bit fast at 57, over that 55 mile per hour speed limit. So even if that had hit the strike zone it would have been a ball.
Tanic likes to wait patiently on this ball — gone. Tanic, opposite field.
He's going to wait on something probably in the 49 mph range. Now on 3–1, you got to think he's got a red light with nobody out still. Make Tanic throw a strike.
It's important to walk there. You want to protect on two strikes, but you got to have strike zone recognition — going down waving at that 3–2 pitch out of the zone.
Plenty of time, knocked it down, still got all day. Five seconds is an eternity. You don't run to first. Five seconds is what you have. Hit the backstop in the air.

They don't run to first — there's just no sense. Five seconds is what you have. You don't want to get in the way of a thrown ball because if a runner gets hit and he's not past a certain point, it's an out.

quotes.tip: Throw must be in the air
quotes.quote: Looks like that one hit the turf just before the backstop. You've got to make that throw in the air in under five seconds. That's going to put him on first with a reached on error.
quotes.who: Booth · short hop is an error

quotes.tip: Don't have to field it clean
quotes.quote: Get that ball — you don't have to field it cleanly, but you just got to get it to that backstop in under five seconds. One of the hallmark rules here in PLW.

Remember to turn that double play — it is the middle part of the backstop, inside those two pipes, or the strike zone. On a regular ground ball the infielders have that entire backstop to aim for. That backstop does play as first base.
quotes.who: Gannon in the booth · Warbirds @ Snappers

quotes.quote: Easy double play as you see him step on third, get the force, throw to second, get the force. You got five seconds upon contact.
quotes.who: Booth · clock starts when the ball is imminent

quotes.quote: He misses the center panel low for the double play. Better to miss low than miss high — don't throw it away and put that runner in scoring position.

quotes.tip: Tag from third: cutoff, then the wall
quotes.quote: The one time that you actually run the bases here in PLW is tagging up from third to home. Only the runner on third can tag up. Fielders just have to get that ball to the backstop or strike zone before the runner touches home. You can use a cutoff guy — catch and a flip.
quotes.who: Gannon in the booth · Warbirds @ Snappers

quotes.quote: The good for the Cajuns is the pitching staff, 100%. When that team does not hit, their pitching staff is going to hold it down. I think that alone is going to be enough to take a team to the championship.

quotes.tip: A walk can settle a pitcher
quotes.quote: Sometimes you need to get that walk out. I talked to Gannon before — and sometimes that walk actually improves your game because it's going to make you pitch even better.
quotes.who: Booth citing Gannon · Ones @ Lightning, Week 17
